hops.query: dependence on third-party foundries such as TSMC for manufacturing supply risk
hops.rationale: The AMD evidence (filter: AMD, filing year 2026, accession 000000248826000018, Item 1A) fully answers the goal of AMD's dependence on third-party foundries such as TSMC for manufacturing supply risk. Passage 16 says AMD uses third-party wafer foundries for all products and relies on TSMC. Passage 17 (adjacent) says TSMC makes all 7nm-and-smaller microprocessor and GPU wafers, GlobalFoundries is relied on for larger nodes, and TSMC, UMC and Samsung supply IC products; it also states supply shortfalls could cause lost sales. Passage 19 covers third-party manufacturer risks such as capacity and delivery limits. Passages 22 and 23 (adjacent) cover yield dependence and name TSMC as the focus for 7nm-and-lower products. Together these state the core facts. The catalog fiscal_period_end does not affect this 2026-filed subquery. No passage is irrelevant, so no retain_ids are needed.

hops.query: capital expenditures for semiconductor manufacturing fabs and capacity
hops.rationale: The TXN 2026 filing passages directly answer the subquery. Item 7 passage-000007 states 2025 capital expenditures of $4.55 billion versus $4.82 billion in 2024, "primarily for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and facilities in both periods," and guides to about $2 to $3 billion in 2026 as the six-year elevated capex cycle nears its end. Passage-000003 repeats the $4.55 billion 2025 capex figure. Passage-000012 and passage-000004 add fab-capacity context: three large-scale 300mm wafer fabs in Sherman, Texas and Lehi, Utah, CHIPS Act funding, and planned capacity expansions that raised manufacturing costs. Together these cover capex for fabs and capacity. The filing scope is correct (TXN, filing year 2026, fiscal 2025 data).

Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2024. Performance summary Our strategic focus is on analog and embedded processing products. We sell our products into the following markets: industrial, automotive, data center, personal electronics and communications equipment. While all of these markets represent good opportunities, we place additional strategic emphasis on designing and selling our products into the industrial, automotive and data center markets, which we believe represent the best long-term growth opportunities. Our focus on analog and embedded processing allows us to generate strong cash flow from operations. Our cash flow from operations of $7.15 billion underscored the strength of our business model, the quality of our product portfolio and the benefit of 300mm production. Free cash flow was $2.94 billion and represented 16.6% of revenue. During 2025, we invested $3.94 billion in R&D and SG&A, invested $4.55 billion in capital expenditures and returned $6.48 billion to shareholders. Macroeconomic factors In 2025, the overall analog and embedded semiconductor market recovery continued, though at a slower pace than prior upturns, likely related to broader macroeconomic dynamics and overall uncertainty. At the same time, global semiconductor shipments remain at levels below the prior peak. In addition, growth of semiconductor content in electronics has continued to drive demand for our products, particularly in the automotive, industrial and data center end markets, and we believe we are well-positioned with inventory and capacity to meet immediate customer demand. U.S. legislative update On July 4, 2025, the U.S. government enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act

(OBBBA). The OBBBA provides changes to U.S. federal tax law, including expensing of U.S. research expenditures and eligible capital expenditures, increasing the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act (CHIPS Act) investment tax credit (ITC) and changing other tax provisions. The effect of the new law resulted in a higher effective tax rate in 2025.
